newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin stable, more active as he fights pneumonia.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin stable, more active as he fights pneumonia.

text.p: President Boris Yeltsin, trying to shake off pneumonia in hospital, was more active and his condition was more stable on Saturday but new speculation surfaced over his ability to govern Russia.

The Kremlin said doctors had examined the 65-year-old president at Moscow's Central Clinical Hospital where he was taken on Wednesday evening with signs of pneumonia, just two months after having heart surgery.
"In their opinion, the patient's condition has stabilised, his activity has grown somewhat," a brief Kremlin statement said. Yeltsin's temperature was normal and his blood pressure stable.
The next official press release on his health was due on Sunday.

The top Kremlin doctor, Sergei Mironov, said on Friday that Yeltsin would have to stay at least another three days in hospital and would need a three-week rest before returning to work in the Kremlin.
He made clear Yeltsin was frustrated by his new illness, which has prevented him re-asserting his power fully.

"Of course I cannot say Boris Nikolayevich feels comfortable spiritually," Mironov told reporters. "Of course this is depressing him, of course his mood is not a very happy one but I see no reason for particular pessimism."

Mironov ruled out any direct link between pneumonia and the quintuple heart bypass which Yeltsin had on November 5, as did pioneering U.S. heart surgeon Michael DeBakey who was a consultant to the Russian surgeons who conducted the operation.
But he added that Yeltsin had been weakened by the operation and should have been admitted to hospital earlier.
The Kremlin has espoused a policy of openness since Yeltsin fell ill. Official statements appear to have been realistic rather than optimistic.

Some political rivals have said Yeltsin should step down and Russian newspapers have taken a gloomy line, expressing doubts over the president's ability to rule the huge country and deal with its many problems.
They named as priorities reform of the demoralised armed forces, payment of long overdue wages and pensions and a dispute with NATO over its enlargement plans.
"Regretfully, it is obvious that the president has no strength left to attend to affairs of the state properly," said the popular liberal Komsomolskaya Pravda newspaper on Saturday.
"Power in Russia is organised in such a way that everything is stuck without aprroval from the very top, be it a president or a general secretary (of the Communist Party)."

Presidential hopeful Alexander Lebed, sacked by Yeltsin as national security adviser last October, said on Friday that the illness had left the country adrift and issued fresh calls for Yeltsin to quit.
Lebed, sacked by Yeltsin for insubordination in October, said the president's new medical setback was turning into a tragedy for the whole country.
"A power vacuum has been created...Now, as never before, it is necessary to rule the country; not to reign but to rule."
Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin, constitutionally number two, was on holiday near Moscow.
Commercial NTV television said the president's chief of staff Anatoly Chubais, reviled by Lebed as a 'regent' wielding vast power, had cancelled a trip to the United States.
Some politicians, uneasy over Yeltsin's long absence, have called for changes in the constitution which gives the president huge powers.

Yegor Stroyev, chairman of the Federation Council Upper House of parliament, made no reference to Yeltsin's illness but called for greater parliamentary control over government appointments and economic policy.

"Many people understand that we cannot simply entrust power to a single person no matter how well we might think of him," liberal deputy Galina Starovoitova told NTV. "We need a redistribution of power between the various branches."
